subtopic_detail: Escalation to IV magnesium after inadequate response to nebulisers
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 24 year old woman with known asthma presenting with a 6 hour deterioration despite home salbutamol every hour. She was hospitalised twice in the last year and takes budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy. She is anxious, speaking in short phrases, and using accessory muscles. Peak expiratory flow is 40 percent of predicted. She has completed 20 minutes of back to back salbutamol and ipratropium via oxygen-driven nebuliser and received oral prednisolone 50 mg 30 minutes ago. Repeat observations show ongoing distress.

Her arterial blood gas shows a normal pCO2 which the intern reports as reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 128/76, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 91% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 36.7
data_table.Chest: widespread expiratory wheeze with reduced air entry bilaterally, no focal signs
data_table.ABG: pH 7.38, pO2 68 mmHg, pCO2 40 mmHg (normal - concerning for exhaustion), HCO3 24 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue salbutamol nebulisers hourly and give a second dose of oral prednisolone 50 mg 4 hours later after further review
options.rationale: After adequate nebulised bronchodilator and oral steroid with no improvement (PEF 40 percent, exhausting pattern with a normal pCO2), escalation to IV magnesium and IV aminophylline consideration plus critical care review is indicated, not merely repeating oral steroid. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes and admit to critical care area with anaesthetic team stand by immediately
options.rationale: Severe asthma exacerbation not responding to standard therapy with signs of exhaustion (normal pCO2 in tachypnoea is pre-arrest) requires IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min, critical care admission, and preparation for possible ventilation. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: Non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP settings at IPAP 12 EPAP 6 as first-line escalation before IV therapy adjuncts
options.rationale: NIV for asthma is limited evidence and not first-line escalation; IV magnesium and consideration of aminophylline precede a decision to intubate rather than NIV in severe asthma. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 200 mg with repeat salbutamol nebuliser and discharge planning if PEF improves to above 60 percent
options.rationale: IV hydrocortisone is a reasonable step but oral prednisolone has already been given and there is no benefit from IV over oral if oral is tolerated; the priority is IV magnesium and critical care escalation given exhaustion. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

options.text: IV adrenaline 500 micrograms subcutaneously for severe bronchospasm as first line escalation for acute presentation today
options.rationale: Adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or peri-arrest asthma; IV magnesium is first-line escalation in severe asthma unresponsive to inhaled bronchodilators and oral steroid. (Source: Australian Asthma Handbook)

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma requires stepwise escalation. Initial therapy is oxygen (target SpO2 93-95 percent), continuous or back to back salbutamol nebuliser plus ipratropium, and oral prednisolone 50 mg (or IV hydrocortisone if not tolerating oral). If no response, escalate to IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min, then consider IV aminophylline or salbutamol infusion with critical care admission. A normal pCO2 in a tachypnoeic patient is a sign of impending respiratory failure and mandates critical care review. Intubation carries high mortality in asthma and is a last resort, ideally with senior anaesthetic input.
key_points: Rising or normal pCO2 in tachypnoea signals exhaustion
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min is first-line escalation
Critical care admission for severe unresponsive asthma
explanation.pearls: Ventilating an asthmatic requires permissive hypercapnia strategy with low tidal volumes (5-6 mL/kg IBW), low respiratory rate (8-10/min), and long expiratory time (I:E 1:4 or greater) to avoid dynamic hyperinflation and pneumothorax.

subtopic: GI bleed on direct oral anticoagulant
subtopic_detail: Reversal choice for apixaban with acute upper GI bleed
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 72 year old woman with atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for stroke prevention. She presents with haematemesis of around 500 mL in the last 4 hours and 2 melaena stools. She last took apixaban this morning 2 hours ago. She has a history of gastric ulcer 5 years ago on aspirin, which is now ceased. Her observations show tachycardia and borderline blood pressure. Endoscopy will be available in 3 hours. Her creatinine is 108 micromol/L and eGFR is 52.

Her bloods show a haemoglobin drop from 118 to 92 g/L since baseline.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 96/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 92 g/L (baseline 118), platelets 202 x10^9/L, INR 1.2, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L
data_table.Medications: apixaban 5 mg BD (last dose 2 hours ago), no aspirin
data_table.Access: two large bore IVs, cross-match 4 units sent, PPI infusion started

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal agent choice?

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 4 units and cryoprecipitate 10 units as reversal of the anticoagulant effect prior to the endoscopy
options.rationale: FFP does not reverse DOACs (no factor deficiency to replace); direct-acting agents are reversed with specific reversal agents or prothrombin complex concentrate. (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

options.text: Andexanet alfa (if available) or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units per kg with activated charcoal 50 g stat
options.rationale: Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor; specific reversal is andexanet alfa (limited AU availability); alternative is 4-factor PCC 50 units/kg; activated charcoal within 2 hours of ingestion reduces further absorption. (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

options.text: IV vitamin K 10 mg with a repeat INR in 6 hours before considering endoscopic intervention this evening in this patient
options.rationale: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not DOACs; apixaban is not a vitamin K antagonist and vitamin K has no effect on it. (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

options.text: IV idarucizumab 5 g given as two 2.5 g doses with a second cross match sample and endoscopy planning within 2 hours
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is the monoclonal antibody Fab fragment that reverses dabigatran (a direct thrombin inhibitor); it has no activity against apixaban (factor Xa inhibitor). (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

options.text: IV tranexamic acid 1 g bolus alone as reversal of the direct oral anticoagulant with rapid onset of therapeutic effect
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic and adjunct in bleeding but does not reverse the anticoagulant effect of DOACs; specific reversal (andexanet or 4-factor PCC) is required. (Source: THANZ 2019 DOAC Reversal)

explanation.summary: DOAC reversal is agent-specific. Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor) is reversed with idarucizumab 5 g (two 2.5 g doses). Apixaban and rivaroxaban (factor Xa inhibitors) are reversed with andexanet alfa where available, or 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate 50 units/kg as alternative. Activated charcoal 50 g reduces absorption if given within 2 hours of ingestion. Standard supportive measures include IV access, fluid and packed cell resuscitation, cessation of the DOAC, treatment of the source (endoscopy for upper GI, embolisation for GI), and PPI infusion for peptic ulcer bleeding.
key_points: Activated charcoal within 2 hours of ingestion
FFP and vitamin K have no role in DOAC reversal
explanation.pearls: The apixaban half-life is around 12 hours; 4-factor PCC (Prothrombinex-VF) contains factors II, VII, IX, X and rapidly restores thrombin generation but does not remove the drug from plasma; andexanet acts as a decoy Xa binding the drug.

subtopic_detail: Second-line agent choice after benzodiazepine failure
stem:
You are the emergency medical registrar reviewing a 42 year old man with known focal epilepsy on levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily. He was brought in with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that has persisted for 12 minutes despite two 10 mg IV midazolam boluses given by paramedics 5 and 10 minutes ago. He continues to seize actively on arrival. He has no known intracranial pathology on prior MRI. Bedside blood glucose is normal. There is no head trauma or intoxication history.

The anaesthetic registrar is 5 minutes away and preparing for possible intubation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 20 with obstructive pattern, SpO2 92% on 15 L Hudson, temperature 37.6
data_table.Bedside tests: glucose 5.6 mmol/L, no head trauma, IV access secured, ECG normal sinus
data_table.Medications: levetiracetam 1500 mg BD (last dose 6 hours ago), no other current medication
data_table.Prior treatment: midazolam 10 mg IV x 2 at 5 and 10 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate second-line agent?

options.text: IV thiopental 5 mg per kg induction with immediate intubation for airway protection and prolonged sedation for the seizure
options.rationale: Thiopental is used in refractory status epilepticus after failed second-line agent; jumping to induction agent skips the effective second-line step and commits to intubation prematurely. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

options.text: IV phenytoin 18 mg per kg loading dose over 30 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia and hypotension
options.rationale: Phenytoin is effective but has cardiac risks (arrhythmia, hypotension) requiring slow infusion and monitoring, and interacts with many drugs; levetiracetam is generally preferred first-choice second-line in AU practice for its safety. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

options.text: IV midazolam infusion 0.1 mg per kg per hour titrated to seizure cessation with intubation for airway protection needs
options.rationale: Midazolam infusion is third-line (refractory status) after failed second-line agent; escalating to infusion without trying a second-line non-benzodiazepine agent commits to intubation prematurely. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

options.text: IV levetiracetam 60 mg per kg loading dose maximum 4500 mg given over 10 minutes with cardiac monitoring during infusion
options.rationale: ESETT trial (2019) showed levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, valproate 40 mg/kg, and fosphenytoin equivalent in second-line status; levetiracetam is preferred in most AU centres for its safety profile, no need for cardiac monitoring beyond basic, and lack of interactions. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate 4 g over 15 minutes as second line agent to address the ongoing seizure activity in this patient
options.rationale: Magnesium is second-line specifically for eclamptic seizures; in status epilepticus without pregnancy, levetiracetam, valproate, or phenytoin are the evidence-based second-line options. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology)

explanation.summary: Status epilepticus management is time-critical. First-line: IV benzodiazepine (midazolam 10 mg IM or IV, lorazepam 4 mg IV, diazepam 10 mg IV; repeat once at 5-10 minutes). Second-line at 20-30 minutes: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (max 4500 mg), sodium valproate 40 mg/kg (max 3000 mg), or phenytoin 20 mg/kg. ESETT trial (2019) showed all three equivalent (around 45 percent seizure termination); levetiracetam is preferred for its safety. Third-line (refractory status) at 40-60 minutes: continuous IV midazolam or propofol infusion with intubation and EEG monitoring. Non-convulsive status warrants EEG-guided titration.
key_points: Refractory (third-line): midazolam or propofol infusion, intubate
Address causes: hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, drug toxicity
explanation.pearls: ESETT (Established Status Epilepticus Treatment Trial, 2019 NEJM) compared fosphenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam as second-line: no difference in seizure termination (around 45-47 percent), and no difference in adverse events; choice is guided by patient factors and centre preference.

subtopic_detail: Chloride burden with renal impairment during first 24 hours
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 34 year old man with type 1 diabetes who presents with 24 hours of vomiting, polyuria, and altered sensorium. He is dehydrated and Kussmaul breathing. His bedside glucose is high and gas confirms severe metabolic acidosis with a large anion gap. The intern has already given 1 L of 0.9 percent saline over 30 minutes. Serum potassium came back at 3.4 mmol/L. He has usually good renal function; today creatinine has risen slightly with a modest calculated eGFR reduction. His fluid balance and hourly urine output monitoring is being organised.

The insulin infusion has not yet been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 106/68, respiratory rate 32 Kussmaul, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9, GCS 13
data_table.Bloods: glucose 32 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, chloride 108 mmol/L, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L (baseline 78), pH 6.98, ketones 6.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next fluid and electrolyte step?

options.text: Give 1 L Hartmann's solution with 20 mmol potassium chloride over 60 minutes before commencing IV insulin infusion therapy
options.rationale: Potassium <3.5 mandates supplementation and delaying insulin until potassium 3.5 or higher; balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's) is preferred to reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis burden of ongoing 0.9 percent saline, particularly with early creatinine rise. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

options.text: Commence IV insulin infusion 0.1 units per kg per hour before further potassium or fluid changes as the priority now
options.rationale: AU DKA protocols delay insulin until potassium is 3.5 or higher to avoid life-threatening hypokalaemia; potassium replacement and continued fluid resuscitation precede insulin in this case. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give another litre of 0.9 percent saline as fluid with 10 mmol potassium chloride and start insulin infusion 0.05 units per kg per hour
options.rationale: Insulin should be delayed until potassium 3.5+; 10 mmol/L is inadequate replacement for K 3.4 with insulin about to run; higher potassium content and delay insulin. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes given the severe acidosis of pH 6.98 as a first line to correct pH now
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is not recommended in DKA at pH >7.0 and has limited role even at pH <6.9 (worsens hypokalaemia, delays ketone clearance); resuscitation with balanced crystalloid and potassium correction is standard. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

options.text: Give 5 percent dextrose 1 L with 40 mmol potassium chloride over 4 hours as fluid choice for the ongoing management now
options.rationale: Dextrose is added when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L to maintain insulin infusion while resolving ketosis; at glucose 32 mmol/L balanced crystalloid without dextrose is appropriate. (Source: ADS Adult DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management follows fluid, potassium, insulin, and ongoing monitoring stages. First fluid is 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 30 min to restore intravascular volume; ADS and increasing evidence favour balanced crystalloid (Hartmann's or Plasmalyte) after the first bolus to reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis, which prolongs anion gap closure. Potassium must be measured before insulin; <3.5 mandates supplementation and delaying insulin; 3.5-5.5 add 20-40 mmol/L KCl to fluids; >5.5 no supplementation until falls. Insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour reduces ketones by around 0.5 mmol/L/hour. Dextrose added when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L. Bicarbonate reserved for pH <6.9 with cardiovascular compromise; even then evidence is limited.
key_points: First bolus 0.9 percent saline, then consider balanced crystalloid
Bicarbonate not routine, even at low pH
explanation.pearls: The PLUS trial (2022 NEJM) in critically ill adults showed no mortality difference between saline and Plasmalyte, but DKA-specific data (SCOPE-DKA, SALT-ED subgroup) suggest balanced fluids may reduce hyperchloraemic acidosis and speed anion gap closure without safety signal.

subtopic_detail: Secondary adrenal insufficiency during illness with atypical timing
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 62 year old man with metastatic melanoma on combination ipilimumab and nivolumab, cycle 3, day 21. He presents with 5 days of worsening lethargy, nausea, vomiting, and postural dizziness. Today he cannot stand without near-syncope. He denies fever or diarrhoea. He is not on regular steroids. His bloods show marked hyponatraemia with normal potassium and hypoglycaemia. Random morning cortisol is markedly low (35 nmol/L) and ACTH is not elevated. TSH is low with low free T4.

He collapses while being transferred from ED trolley to ward bed.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128 supine, 148 sitting, blood pressure 88/54 supine, 68/40 sitting, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.5
data_table.Bloods: sodium 118 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L, urea 8.4 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, cortisol 35 nmol/L (>500 stress-normal), ACTH 2 pmol/L (2-11 normal, low here), TSH 0.4 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L
data_table.Medications: combination ipilimumab plus nivolumab (day 21 of cycle 3), paracetamol PRN
data_table.Prior: no diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency, no chronic steroids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, then 100 mg 6 hourly, plus 5 percent dextrose in 0.9 percent saline resuscitation
options.rationale: Combined hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, postural collapse, low cortisol with normal potassium and low ACTH (secondary AI from ipilimumab-induced hypophysitis) is adrenal crisis; treatment is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 6 hourly and IV dextrose in saline resuscitation; also need to consider levothyroxine after cortisol has been replaced (never before, to avoid precipitating crisis). (Source: RCH-based eTG Adrenal Crisis and Endocrine Society Immune Endocrinopathy Guidelines)

options.text: IV levothyroxine 500 micrograms loading dose given the low TSH and low free T4 as first line prior to any steroid
options.rationale: Giving levothyroxine before cortisol replacement in coexisting secondary AI precipitates adrenal crisis by increasing metabolic demand for cortisol; steroid must be given first. (Source: eTG Complete Endocrinology)

options.text: IV normal saline 2 L over 4 hours with hypertonic saline 3 percent for the hyponatraemia and monitoring before steroid
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for seizures or symptomatic severe hyponatraemia; adrenal-crisis hyponatraemia corrects with volume resuscitation plus cortisol replacement, and giving hypertonic without cortisol risks osmotic demyelination and delays treatment. (Source: eTG Complete Endocrinology)

options.text: IV dexamethasone 8 mg alone as steroid replacement with 0.9 percent saline resuscitation and endocrine review tomorrow
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and does not allow subsequent Synacthen testing; hydrocortisone is the correct steroid for adrenal crisis. (Source: eTG Complete Endocrinology)

options.text: Ceasing checkpoint inhibitor therapy alone with observation on cardiac monitor and endocrine referral within 24 hours
options.rationale: Cessation of the offending agent is required but does not treat the acute crisis; IV hydrocortisone is life-saving and must not be delayed. (Source: eTG Complete Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Immune checkpoint inhibitor endocrinopathies include hypothyroidism (nivolumab), hypophysitis with secondary AI (ipilimumab, especially combination therapy), and less often type 1 diabetes. Adrenal crisis in this setting is characterised by hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypotension, low cortisol with inappropriately normal or low ACTH (secondary), and often coexisting central hypothyroidism. Treatment is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 100 mg 6 hourly (mineralocorticoid activity at these doses is adequate); IV volume resuscitation with dextrose-containing crystalloid; correct precipitants; withhold checkpoint inhibitor pending endocrine review. Coexisting central hypothyroidism requires cortisol replacement first, then levothyroxine.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 6 hourly
Never give levothyroxine before cortisol in coexisting AI
explanation.pearls: Baseline morning cortisol >500 nmol/L rules out AI; <100 nmol/L makes it likely; 100-500 nmol/L needs Synacthen (250 mcg tetracosactrin) testing with 30 and 60 minute cortisol, though in secondary AI the adrenal has not yet atrophied so response can be preserved acutely.

sources.label: ESMO Immune Related Adverse Events Guidelines

subtopic: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state with mixed DKA features
subtopic_detail: Fluid strategy when osmolality and ketosis both present
stem:
You are the intensive care registrar reviewing a 68 year old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and empagliflozin who was found by his wife drowsy and confused. He had been unwell with a chest infection for 5 days, with reduced oral intake. On arrival his glucose is markedly high with an elevated calculated osmolality; he also has mild ketosis and a bicarbonate at the lower end of normal with a raised anion gap. His creatinine is significantly elevated over baseline. He is severely dehydrated with tachycardia and hypotension. GCS is 12.

He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and moderate left ventricular systolic dysfunction.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 26 mildly Kussmaul, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.6, GCS 12
data_table.Bloods: glucose 44 mmol/L, sodium 152 mmol/L (measured; corrected 160), potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 88), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, ketones 3.2 mmol/L, pH 7.28, calculated osmolality 348 mmol/kg
data_table.Medications: metformin, empagliflozin, atorvastatin, perindopril, bisoprolol, aspirin
data_table.Estimated fluid deficit: 8-10 L based on osmolar picture and dehydration signs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid strategy?

options.text: IV 5 percent dextrose 1 L with insulin 0.1 units per kg per hour as an initial approach because ketones are present now
options.rationale: Dextrose is added when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L; starting with dextrose at glucose 44 mmol/L is inappropriate and does not correct volume deficit. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 2 L over 30 minutes with insulin infusion 0.1 units per kg per hour as standard DKA fluid strategy today
options.rationale: HHS-predominant with corrected sodium 160 requires slower fluid replacement over 24-48 hours (aim sodium reduction <=10 mmol/L per 24 hours) to avoid cerebral oedema; standard DKA-rate fluids risk osmotic demyelination and cerebral oedema. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

options.text: IV 0.45 percent saline 2 L over 60 minutes as the primary resuscitation fluid to correct hyperosmolality first now today
options.rationale: 0.45 percent saline as bolus can cause too-rapid sodium correction and cerebral oedema; first resuscitation uses 0.9 percent saline at controlled rate, switching to 0.45 percent later based on corrected sodium and osmolality changes. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

options.text: IV 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 60 minutes with insulin infusion 0.05 units per kg per hour and euglycaemic DKA precautions applied
options.rationale: Mixed HHS with SGLT2-inhibitor-associated euglycaemic DKA features requires slower fluid replacement in HHS-predominant picture (osmolality 348, sodium 152, corrected sodium 160) to avoid cerebral oedema, plus low-dose insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour and delayed ketone clearance strategy; empagliflozin ceased. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

options.text: Hartmann's solution 2 L over 60 minutes with immediate insulin bolus of 0.15 units per kg to bring glucose down rapidly
options.rationale: Rapid fluid and insulin in HHS with high corrected sodium risks cerebral oedema; controlled rehydration and low-dose insulin are safer; a bolus of insulin is not recommended in HHS. (Source: ADS HHS Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Mixed HHS with euglycaemic DKA (or overt DKA) features requires an HHS-predominant strategy when osmolality and corrected sodium are the driving issues. Fluid replacement is slower than DKA to avoid cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination: aim sodium reduction <=10 mmol/L per 24 hours and osmolality reduction <=3 mmol/kg per hour. Use 0.9 percent saline first, switching to 0.45 percent saline when corrected sodium rises further despite therapy. Insulin at 0.05 units/kg/hour (lower than standard DKA) sufficient because SGLT2-inhibitor-associated euglycaemic DKA has slower ketone clearance and increased ketone production risk. Empagliflozin ceased. VBG and osmolality every 2-4 hours guide titration.
explanation.pearls: Corrected sodium formula: measured sodium + 0.3 x (glucose - 5.5) mmol/L (Katz correction) or the older 2.4 factor per 5.5 mmol/L glucose above 5.5; monitor real (not measured) sodium as glucose falls, because it will rise; anticipate potassium falling as insulin acts.
